summary: Ken Pogran discusses how to give limited free access to file transfer servers, for example for mail, without assuming one particular scheme for access control. He argues that earlier proposals such as Bressler's in RFC 487 presume how authentication works, which different systems implement differently.

plainLanguage.summary: This note examines the issues behind offering limited free access to file-transfer servers. It argues that proposals should distinguish proving a user's identity, checking file permissions and deciding who pays.

questions: principle of least privilege ftp server
what does rfc 501 say about free file transfer
subtitle: A critique of free file-transfer proposals that separate authentication, file access and accounting.

tldr.problem: Proposals for free file transfer mix user authentication, file access control and accounting, and may assume mechanisms that some hosts do not use.
tldr.mechanism: The author compares two ways to run a file-transfer server and questions who should be charged for transfers and what account should pay.
tldr.outcome: The note does not offer a replacement design; it calls for clearer discussion of how different systems handle authentication and access control.

today: The unit metadata records RFC 501's status as Unknown and lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The document is commentary on free file-transfer proposals, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: Three Issues Behind Free File Transfer
sections.content:
Ken Pogran says that access control, user authentication and accounting are becoming important as the ARPA Network matures. Proposals for login-less mail, free accounts or free file transfer often assume particular ways to handle these issues, which can conflict with how different host systems work.

The RFC criticizes Bressler's file-transfer proposal, discussing RFC 487, for mixing file access controls with system authentication and for making assumptions about accounting. Pogran says this note is only a partial discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Offering file transfer without a normal login raises three separate questions: who the user is, which files they may use and who pays for the work.

sections.title: Which Identity the Server Uses
sections.content:
The author describes two ways to run a File Transfer Server. A system daemon can use a highly privileged system identity and check the user's file access itself. Or the server process can use the user's own principal identifier so the ordinary file-system rules check access.

The RFC says the proposal it discusses assumes the daemon approach. It notes that using the user's identifier follows the principle of least privilege: a process should have only the access it needs. A footnote says that this approach may require a USER, PASS and possibly ACCT authentication sequence before file transfers.
sections.plainLanguage: A file server can act with broad system privileges or with the user's own permissions. Using the user's permissions lets normal file-system checks decide what the server can access.

sections.title: Who Pays for the Transfer
sections.content:
Pogran questions whether a recipient should pay for the CPU and I/O used when someone else sends a file into the recipient's directory. He also questions how an unauthenticated user could tell a server to charge another person's account. He suggests that a general Network services account may be more appropriate; the note points to RFC 491 for mechanisms.

The author also argues that system-overhead accounts cannot be assumed to exist or be appropriate on every host. Charging transfers to local overhead could pass costs to customers who are not interested in the ARPA Network. A file server may also be unable to distinguish system files from user files by pathname.
sections.plainLanguage: The author asks whether the recipient, sender or a shared network-services account should pay. He says one accounting rule may not fit every host.

sections.title: The Wider Design Concern
sections.content:
The author argues that network-wide mechanisms are difficult to design without assuming how each host implements authentication, access controls and accounting. He asks the network community to discuss how systems handle these issues before proposing shared mechanisms.

A note describes both a sender-push and recipient-pull approach to transferring a file. The author says either arrangement raises questions about authorization and charging, and points to other work for further discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Different hosts use different security and accounting arrangements. A shared file-transfer service must account for those differences instead of assuming every host works the same way.

references.text: Bressler, B., the free file-transfer proposal discussed by Pogran, RFC 487.
RFC 491, cited for mechanisms to charge a Network services account.
RFC 354, cited in a footnote for an FTP authentication sequence.
